questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the law intervenes to protect consumers rather than leaving them to rely on the principle of 'buyer beware'?
options: Consumers are legally unable to read or negotiate any contract without a lawyer being present
Common law has never allowed a buyer to sue a seller for selling faulty goods
Businesses are presumed to act dishonestly unless they can prove otherwise in court
Businesses usually know far more about their products and contract terms than consumers do
questions.explanation: Consumer protection responds to an imbalance of information and bargaining power between businesses and consumers, which caveat emptor ignores. Consumers can read and negotiate contracts themselves, and the law makes no presumption of dishonesty; it sets minimum standards instead.

questions.stem: Which international instrument, first adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1985, sets out principles that member states are encouraged to follow in protecting consumers?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The United Nations Guidelines for Consumer Protection
The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods
questions.explanation: The UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection were adopted in 1985 and later revised, most fully in 2015, to cover areas such as e-commerce and financial services. They are non-binding guidelines, not a treaty. The Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods governs sales between businesses, not consumer protection.

questions.stem: Where is the Australian Consumer Law found?
options: In Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth)
In Part IV of the Fair Trading Act 1987 (NSW) as a separate code
In the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (Cth)
In the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001 (Cth)
questions.explanation: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL) is Schedule 2 of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), which replaced the Trade Practices Act 1974. The Fair Trading Act 1987 (NSW) applies the ACL as a law of NSW rather than containing its own separate code.

questions.stem: Leila believes her bank's credit card was sold to her using misleading claims. Which regulator, rather than the ACCC, is mainly responsible for consumer protection in financial services like this?
options: The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA)
The Commonwealth Ombudsman, through its consumer complaints service
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)
questions.explanation: Financial products and credit are largely carved out of the ACL, and parallel consumer protections in the ASIC Act and credit laws are enforced by ASIC. APRA supervises the financial soundness of banks and insurers rather than how products are marketed to consumers, and NCAT is a tribunal, not a regulator.

questions.stem: Which NSW body hears and decides consumer claims between consumers and traders, through its Consumer and Commercial Division?
options: The District Court of NSW, Civil Division
The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT)
The Land and Environment Court of NSW
The NSW Ombudsman, through its consumer disputes branch
questions.explanation: NCAT's Consumer and Commercial Division resolves consumer claims about goods and services cheaply and with less formality than a court. The NSW Ombudsman investigates complaints about public sector agencies, not disputes with private traders.

questions.stem: Three months after Sam buys a new phone, it stops charging even though he has looked after it. The store tells him to deal with the manufacturer. Under the ACL, which is correct?
options: The store must provide a remedy because the phone may fail the guarantee of acceptable quality
Sam can only seek a remedy from the manufacturer once the store's warranty has ended
Sam has no remedy at all, because consumer guarantees end once the goods have been used
The store must refund Sam only if he bought an extended warranty at the time of sale
questions.explanation: The consumer guarantee of acceptable quality requires goods to be durable and free from defects for a reasonable time, and the retailer that sold them must provide a remedy. Consumer guarantees apply automatically, regardless of any warranty, and cannot be avoided by referring the consumer to the manufacturer.

questions.stem: A washing machine floods Priya's laundry on its first use because of a serious defect, so a reasonable consumer would not have bought it had they known. What is Priya entitled to under the ACL?
options: Only damages for the floor, because the machine can still be fixed by a technician
Nothing until she has given the supplier three attempts to repair the machine
To choose a refund or a replacement, because this is a major failure
Only a repair at first, because the supplier chooses the remedy for any failure
questions.explanation: A failure is major if a reasonable consumer fully aware of the problem would not have bought the goods, and then the consumer chooses between a refund and a replacement (and may also claim reasonably foreseeable loss). For a minor failure the supplier may choose to repair instead, and the ACL sets no rule requiring three repair attempts.

questions.stem: A shop displays a sign reading 'No refunds under any circumstances'. Why does this sign breach the ACL?
options: Shops must give refunds whenever a customer simply changes their mind about goods
Signs about refunds must be approved by Fair Trading NSW before they are displayed
Only online retailers may limit refunds, so a physical shop cannot display such a sign
Consumer guarantees cannot be excluded, so the sign misrepresents consumers' rights
questions.explanation: Consumers' rights to remedies under the consumer guarantees cannot be excluded by contract or notice, so the sign misleads consumers about those rights. There is no right to a refund for a mere change of mind, which is why a sign limiting change-of-mind refunds is lawful.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an element of the test for whether a term in a standard form consumer contract is unfair?
options: It was written by the business rather than negotiated by a lawyer for the consumer
It was printed in a font smaller than the rest of the contract's main terms
It appears in a contract that the consumer has signed on paper rather than online
It would cause a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations
questions.explanation: A term is unfair if it would cause a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations, is not reasonably necessary to protect the business's legitimate interests, and would cause detriment if relied on. Who drafted the contract, the font size and the signing method are not part of the test, though transparency is considered.

questions.stem: A gym's standard form contract lets the gym raise fees at any time without notice, while members can never cancel. Since November 2023, what consequence follows if a court finds the term unfair?
options: The gym commits a criminal offence and its directors face terms of imprisonment
The term is void and the gym can also face a civil penalty for including it
The whole contract becomes void and every member must receive a full refund
The term stays binding unless each member had objected to it before signing
questions.explanation: An unfair term in a standard form consumer or small business contract is void, and since 9 November 2023 proposing, using or relying on such a term can attract civil penalties. The rest of the contract continues if it can operate without the term, and the regime is civil rather than criminal.

questions.stem: A salesperson knocks on Tom's door uninvited and he signs a contract for solar panels worth several thousand dollars. What protection does the ACL give him?
options: A cooling-off period of 10 business days in which he can cancel the agreement
A cooling-off period of 24 hours, after which the agreement is fully binding
No protection, because he chose to sign the contract while he was at home
A right to cancel at any time during the first year of the solar panel contract
questions.explanation: An agreement negotiated through an uninvited visit is an unsolicited consumer agreement, which carries a 10 business day cooling-off period. The ACL also restricts the hours of door-to-door selling and requires the salesperson to leave when asked.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of CHOICE in promoting consumer interests?
options: It hears consumer disputes and makes binding orders for refunds and repairs
It issues mandatory safety standards that all suppliers of goods must follow
It tests products, publishes findings and lobbies government for law reform
It prosecutes businesses that breach the ACL in the Federal Court of Australia
questions.explanation: CHOICE is an independent, not-for-profit consumer organisation that tests products, informs consumers and advocates for reform. It has no power to prosecute, adjudicate or make standards; those functions belong to the ACCC and state regulators, NCAT, and the Commonwealth Minister.

questions.stem: A current affairs program exposes a car dealer's misleading finance practices, and many viewers complain to regulators. Which is the most accurate assessment of the media's role here?
options: It has no legitimate role, because only courts may comment on alleged breaches of the ACL
It can prompt investigation and reform, but it cannot itself provide consumers with legal remedies
It provides the main enforcement mechanism because regulators act only after a media report
It replaces the need for regulators because public exposure alone forces businesses to comply
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism raises awareness and can push regulators and governments to act, but individual consumers still need a regulator, NCAT or a court to obtain a remedy. Regulators also act on complaints and their own investigations, so the media is a catalyst rather than the enforcement mechanism.

questions.stem: A company accidentally prints the wrong battery life in its advertisement for a laptop. Can it still breach section 18 of the ACL, which prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct?
options: Yes, but only if a consumer had already been charged under criminal law for it
Yes, because section 18 does not require any intention to mislead consumers
No, because section 18 applies only when a business deliberately lies to buyers
No, because section 18 covers only spoken statements and not printed advertising
questions.explanation: Section 18 asks whether the conduct, viewed as a whole, is misleading or deceptive or likely to mislead or deceive; the business's intention is irrelevant. It covers any conduct in trade or commerce, including print and online advertising, and is enforced through civil remedies.

questions.stem: A store advertises televisions at a very low price, but stocks only two and has no intention of offering a reasonable quantity. Which ACL prohibition does this conduct most directly breach?
options: Component pricing
Bait advertising
Referral selling
Pyramid selling
questions.explanation: Bait advertising is advertising goods or services at a specified price when the supplier does not intend to offer them at that price for a reasonable period and in reasonable quantities. Referral selling offers a rebate for referring other customers, and component pricing concerns failing to show the total price.

questions.stem: An airline website advertises a fare of $99 in large print, then adds a compulsory booking fee and taxes at checkout. What does the ACL require?
options: The airline must remove the booking fee, because all such fees are unlawful
The single total price must be shown at least as prominently as any part price
Compulsory fees may be added at checkout as long as they are listed somewhere on the website
Only the base fare needs to be shown, because taxes are set by the government
questions.explanation: The ACL's component pricing rule requires a business that advertises part of a price to also state the single total price, as prominently as the part price, including compulsory fees and charges. Booking fees themselves are not banned, but they must be included in the total price.

questions.stem: A salesperson gains entry to elderly people's homes by offering a free vacuum cleaner check, then pressures them into buying expensive vacuum cleaners. A Full Federal Court found similar conduct to be:
options: a minor breach of the consumer guarantee that goods match their description
a criminal fraud that the ACL itself has no power to deal with or remedy
unconscionable conduct in connection with the supply of goods or services
conduct permitted by the ACL, because each buyer signed a written contract
questions.explanation: In ACCC v Lux Distributors (2013), the Full Federal Court held that this kind of conduct towards elderly women was unconscionable under the ACL. Statutory unconscionable conduct looks at all the circumstances, including the parties' relative bargaining strength and any pressure or unfair tactics, so a signed contract is no defence.

questions.stem: A social media influencer posts glowing reviews of a skincare brand without disclosing that the brand paid for the posts. Why can this create a problem under the ACL?
options: Only television advertising is regulated, so the brand rather than the influencer is liable
Paid posts must be registered with Fair Trading NSW before they are allowed to be published
Hiding the commercial relationship can mislead consumers about whether the review is independent
Influencers are banned from accepting any payment for posts that mention a consumer product by name
questions.explanation: Presenting paid content as an independent review can be misleading or deceptive conduct, or a false representation, because consumers give more weight to genuine testimonials. Paid promotion itself is lawful, and the ACL applies to conduct in trade or commerce in any medium, including online.

questions.stem: How does the role of Ad Standards, which administers advertising industry codes, differ from that of the ACCC?
options: Ad Standards decisions bind courts, so the ACCC must follow them in any later proceedings
Ad Standards relies on voluntary compliance with its panel's findings and cannot impose fines
Ad Standards can prosecute breaches of the ACL, but the ACCC deals only with industry codes
Ad Standards sets the ACL's penalties, while the ACCC handles complaints about taste and decency
questions.explanation: Advertising codes are a form of industry self-regulation: the Ad Standards Community Panel can find an advertisement in breach, but it relies on advertisers withdrawing it and cannot fine them. The ACCC enforces the ACL as a statutory regulator and can take businesses to court for penalties.

questions.stem: Which website, run by the National Anti-Scam Centre within the ACCC, lets people report scams and learn about current scam types?
options: Moneysmart
Product Safety Australia
Lawstuff
Scamwatch
questions.explanation: Scamwatch is run by the National Anti-Scam Centre, which was set up within the ACCC in 2023. Moneysmart is ASIC's financial guidance website, and Product Safety Australia publishes recalls and safety warnings.

questions.stem: Why are scams that originate overseas particularly difficult for Australian consumer law to address?
options: Scam victims are not allowed to report losses to any Australian authority if the scammer is overseas
Offenders may be outside Australian jurisdiction, so they are hard to identify, prosecute or recover money from
Australian law does not treat scams as unlawful unless the victim lost a very large amount of money
The ACL applies only to goods bought in physical shops, so online scams fall outside its coverage
questions.explanation: Scammers based overseas can be impossible to locate, and Australian courts and regulators cannot easily enforce orders abroad, so money is rarely recovered. That is why responses focus on prevention, such as disruption, warnings and obligations on banks, telcos and digital platforms, rather than prosecution alone.

questions.stem: Which Act sets up the national scheme regulating consumer credit, including licensing of credit providers and responsible lending?
options: The Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth), Schedule 2
The Fair Trading Act 1987 (NSW)
The Corporations Act 2001 (Cth)
The National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (Cth)
questions.explanation: The National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (Cth) requires credit providers and brokers to hold an Australian credit licence and imposes responsible lending obligations; its Schedule 1 is the National Credit Code. It is administered by ASIC, not the ACCC.

questions.stem: Under responsible lending obligations, what must a lender do before giving a consumer a credit card?
options: Confirm only that the consumer is over 18 and holds an Australian bank account in their own name
Obtain a guarantee from a family member for every consumer who earns less than the average weekly wage
Refer the consumer to a financial counsellor and wait for written approval before lending money
Make reasonable inquiries, verify the consumer's finances and assess whether the credit is unsuitable
questions.explanation: Licensees must make reasonable inquiries about the consumer's requirements, objectives and financial situation, take reasonable steps to verify it, and assess whether the credit is unsuitable, for example because repayments would cause substantial hardship. Age and a bank account alone are not enough, and guarantees or counselling are not required.

questions.stem: After losing his job, Ahmed cannot keep up his car loan repayments. What can he do under the National Credit Code?
options: Stop paying immediately, because job loss cancels any consumer credit contract
Apply to NCAT to have the whole loan written off because he is now unemployed and has no income
Nothing, because hardship applies only to home loans and not to car loans
Ask the lender for a hardship variation, such as reduced or postponed repayments
questions.explanation: A borrower in financial hardship can ask the credit provider to vary the contract, for example by extending the term or postponing payments, and the lender must respond. Job loss does not cancel the debt, and if the lender refuses he can complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA)?
options: A court that hears criminal prosecutions for breaches of consumer credit laws
A charity that lends money to consumers who have been refused credit by banks
A free external dispute resolution scheme for complaints against financial firms
A government department that sets interest rates for credit cards and loans
questions.explanation: AFCA began on 1 November 2018 as a single, free ombudsman scheme for complaints about banks, lenders, insurers and other financial firms, which must be members. Its decisions bind the firm if the consumer accepts them. It does not set interest rates or hear prosecutions.

questions.stem: A Year 12 student finds she can buy clothes using a 'buy now, pay later' app with almost no checks. Which statement about the law on such products is accurate?
options: Since 2025 most such providers must hold a credit licence and meet modified responsible lending rules
Such products have always been banned for anyone under 21 by the National Consumer Credit Protection Act
Such products are regulated only by voluntary codes, with no role for ASIC in their oversight
Such products are treated as gifts from the retailer, so missed payments cannot be recovered at all
questions.explanation: From 10 June 2025, buy now, pay later contracts were brought under the national credit laws, so providers need an Australian credit licence, must belong to AFCA and must meet modified responsible lending obligations. Before then, the industry relied largely on a voluntary code, which critics saw as weak protection for young and vulnerable consumers.

questions.stem: ASIC finds that a payday lender repeatedly lent to customers it knew could not repay. Which enforcement response is available to ASIC under the credit laws?
options: Sentencing the lender's directors to imprisonment without any court proceedings at all
Fixing the interest rate that every Australian lender must charge on small loans
Seeking civil penalties in court and cancelling or suspending the lender's credit licence
Ordering the lender's customers to repay their loans directly to ASIC instead of the lender
questions.explanation: ASIC can take civil penalty proceedings, cancel or suspend an Australian credit licence, make banning orders, issue infringement notices and accept enforceable undertakings. Only a court can impose imprisonment after a criminal prosecution, and ASIC does not set lenders' interest rates.

questions.stem: Why are free financial counselling services, such as those reached through the National Debt Helpline, important for vulnerable consumers?
options: They can cancel a consumer's debts on the spot, without needing the lender's agreement or any court order
They make binding rulings on credit disputes that the lender must follow immediately
They lend money at low interest so that consumers can repay their other debts
They help people negotiate with creditors and understand their rights when they cannot afford a lawyer
questions.explanation: Financial counsellors give free, independent advice, help consumers apply for hardship arrangements and negotiate with creditors, and refer them to legal help or AFCA. They cannot cancel debts or make binding rulings, which require the creditor's agreement or a dispute resolution body.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a mandatory and a voluntary product standard in Australia?
options: A mandatory standard is legally enforceable, while a voluntary standard is followed by choice
A mandatory standard applies only to imports, while a voluntary standard applies to local goods
A mandatory standard is set by industry, while a voluntary standard is set by the Parliament
A mandatory standard covers food only, while a voluntary standard covers all other products
questions.explanation: Mandatory safety and information standards are made under the ACL, and supplying goods that do not comply is unlawful. Voluntary standards, many published by Standards Australia, are best practice that suppliers can choose to follow unless a law adopts them.

questions.stem: After young children were seriously injured and killed by swallowing button batteries, what was the regulatory response under the ACL?
options: A permanent ban on the sale of all products containing batteries of any size
A rule making parents criminally liable whenever a child swallows a battery
Mandatory safety and information standards requiring secure battery compartments and warnings
A voluntary industry code that suppliers could choose to adopt if they wished to do so
questions.explanation: Mandatory button battery standards took effect in June 2022, requiring secure compartments, child-resistant packaging and warnings. Regulators judged that voluntary measures had not been enough, but they did not ban all battery-powered products.

questions.stem: A supplier learns that a toy it sells has caused a serious injury to a child. What is its obligation under the ACL?
options: To report it only if the injured child's parents first make a formal complaint to the supplier
To report it within twelve months in the supplier's annual report to its shareholders
To report it only if the toy was manufactured in Australia rather than imported from an overseas factory
To report it to the Commonwealth Minister, through the ACCC, within two days of becoming aware
questions.explanation: Mandatory reporting requires a supplier to notify the Commonwealth Minister, in practice via the ACCC, within two days of becoming aware that a consumer good it supplied caused or may have caused a death, serious injury or illness. The duty applies whether the product was made locally or imported.

questions.stem: When Takata airbags were found to be dangerous and some manufacturers' voluntary recalls had been too slow, what step did the Commonwealth take in 2018?
options: It issued a voluntary standard asking manufacturers to consider replacing the airbags
It permanently banned the sale of all motor vehicles fitted with any type of airbag
It made each car owner responsible for paying to replace the affected airbags
It issued a compulsory recall notice requiring the affected airbags to be replaced
questions.explanation: The Takata recall was made compulsory in 2018 because the voluntary recall was not effectively addressing the risk, making suppliers responsible for replacing the affected airbags at no cost to owners. A compulsory recall is a stronger response than a voluntary recall and is narrower than a ban on all airbags.

questions.stem: Which statement about product bans under the ACL is correct?
options: A state minister can impose an interim ban, but only the Commonwealth Minister can impose a permanent ban
Only NCAT can impose a ban, and it must first hear from every supplier of the product in Australia
A ban applies only to products made in Australia, because imported goods are dealt with by customs
Any consumer can impose a ban by lodging a complaint with Fair Trading NSW about a product
questions.explanation: Interim bans can be imposed by the Commonwealth Minister or a state or territory minister to deal quickly with a risk, while a permanent ban is a Commonwealth decision applying nationally. Bans are imposed by ministers rather than tribunals, and they apply to imported and local goods alike.

questions.stem: Why does a globalised market make product safety harder to enforce?
options: Australian product safety laws do not apply to any goods that were manufactured outside Australia
Overseas manufacturers must follow Australian standards, so local regulators no longer check products
International trade agreements prevent Australia from recalling goods that were imported legally
Consumers buy directly from overseas online sellers who may be beyond the reach of Australian regulators
questions.explanation: Products bought online from overseas sellers may never pass through an Australian business that can be held responsible, so recalls and penalties are hard to apply. Australian safety laws still apply to goods supplied in Australia, and imported goods can be recalled and banned.

questions.stem: Why does the law seek to protect competition in the marketplace?
options: Competition tends to lower prices, widen choice and encourage better quality and innovation
Competition guarantees that every business in a market will make an equal profit each year
Competition allows the government to set the prices of most goods and services directly
Competition removes the need for any consumer protection laws such as the Australian Consumer Law
questions.explanation: When businesses compete for customers, they have an incentive to cut prices, improve quality and offer more choice. Competition law does not guarantee equal profits or let government set prices, and consumer protection laws are still needed alongside it.

questions.stem: Which conduct is prohibited as cartel conduct under Part IV of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth)?
options: Two companies forming a joint venture approved by the ACCC
A supplier choosing to sell only through its own online store
Competitors agreeing on the prices they will charge customers
A business lowering its prices to win customers from rivals
questions.explanation: Cartel conduct includes price fixing, restricting output, sharing markets and bid rigging by competitors, and serious cartel conduct is a criminal offence as well as a civil contravention. Lowering prices independently is the competition the law wants to encourage.

questions.stem: Three building companies secretly agree which of them will win a council tender, with the other two submitting deliberately higher bids. This is an example of:
options: misuse of market power by the council
bid rigging, which is a form of cartel conduct
resale price maintenance by the companies
exclusive dealing between the companies and the council
questions.explanation: Competitors arranging who will win a tender and submitting cover bids is bid rigging, one of the forms of cartel conduct that can lead to criminal prosecution. Resale price maintenance involves a supplier controlling the price at which resellers sell its goods.

questions.stem: Under section 46 of the Competition and Consumer Act, what must be shown for a business to have misused its market power?
options: It has made a profit greater than its rivals and has advertised more often than they have in that market
It has a substantial degree of market power and its conduct has the purpose, effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition
It has the largest market share in Australia and has charged a higher price than any of its competitors
It has a monopoly in a market and has refused to sell at the price that its customers have requested
questions.explanation: Since 2017, section 46 prohibits a corporation with a substantial degree of market power from engaging in conduct that has the purpose, effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition. Size, high prices or high profits are not unlawful in themselves; the test focuses on the harm to competition.

questions.stem: How does the ACCC's immunity policy help it to detect secret cartels?
options: It allows the ACCC to search any business premises without a warrant whenever a cartel is suspected
It guarantees every cartel member immunity from penalties if they agree to stop the conduct
It requires all businesses to report their prices to the ACCC each month for comparison
The first cartel member to report and fully cooperate may avoid proceedings, which gives members a reason to break ranks
questions.explanation: Cartels are secret and hard to prove, so the ACCC offers conditional immunity from civil proceedings, and can recommend criminal immunity to the CDPP, to the first party that reports and cooperates. Immunity is not available to every member, which creates a race to confess.

questions.stem: Under the merger regime that began on 1 January 2026, what must the parties to a large acquisition that meets the notification thresholds do?
options: Seek approval from the Federal Court, which decides all mergers without the ACCC
Obtain the consent of each of their customers before announcing the proposed deal
Notify the ACCC and not complete the deal until the ACCC has cleared it
Complete the deal first and inform the ACCC within twelve months of completion
questions.explanation: The mandatory and suspensory regime requires acquisitions above the thresholds to be notified to the ACCC, and they cannot be completed until cleared. Under the old system notification was voluntary, and the ACCC had to go to court to stop a merger it thought would substantially lessen competition.
